difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a necessary/sufficient confusion — treating a sufficient condition as necessary. Each answer choice is a dense mini-argument, and two trap choices (B and D) involve conditional reasoning that superficially resembles the flaw but differs in directionality or conclusion strength.
stimulus: Any medication that has been approved by the Food and Drug Administration has undergone rigorous clinical trials. Veloxaril has undergone rigorous clinical trials. Therefore, Veloxaril has almost certainly been approved by the Food and Drug Administration.
questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All licensed structural engineers have passed a state certification examination. Marcelline has passed a state certification examination. Therefore, Marcelline is almost certainly a licensed structural engineer.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every tenured professor at this university has published peer-reviewed research. Professor Hendricks has not published peer-reviewed research. Therefore, Professor Hendricks is almost certainly not tenured.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only students who have completed the prerequisite course may enroll in Advanced Topology. Since Devraj has completed the prerequisite course, he will almost certainly enroll in Advanced Topology.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some award-winning architects have never taken a formal design course. Quintero has never taken a formal design course. Therefore, Quintero is almost certainly an award-winning architect.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whenever a bridge design passes a federal safety review, it is eligible for public funding. The Harmon Bridge design passed a federal safety review. Therefore, the Harmon Bridge design is almost certainly eligible for public funding.

explanations.correct: Stimulus structure: All FDA-approved drugs → rigorous trials; Veloxaril → rigorous trials; therefore Veloxaril → FDA-approved. This affirms the consequent: the sufficient condition (FDA approval) guarantees the necessary condition (trials), but having the necessary condition does not confirm the sufficient condition. Choice A replicates this exactly: All licensed engineers → passed exam; Marcelline → passed exam; therefore Marcelline → licensed engineer. Same affirming-the-consequent flaw with matching probabilistic conclusion strength.
explanations.A: Correct. Matches the affirming-the-consequent flaw precisely: the universal conditional runs from licensed engineer to passed exam, and the argument observes the consequent (passed exam) to conclude the antecedent (licensed engineer).
explanations.B: This is a valid modus tollens inference, not a flaw. If all tenured professors published and Hendricks did not publish, the conclusion that Hendricks is not tenured follows validly.
explanations.C: This confuses a necessary condition ('only students who completed the prerequisite may enroll') with a sufficient condition, concluding the student will enroll. The logical structure differs: it treats a necessary condition as sufficient, which is the converse of the stimulus's error.
explanations.D: The premise uses 'some,' not 'all,' so the flaw is a different one — drawing a conclusion about an individual from an existential claim, not from a universal conditional. The stimulus's flaw depends on a universal (all) statement.
explanations.E: This is a valid inference. The conditional 'whenever passes review → eligible for funding' is affirmed by the antecedent (passes review), and the conclusion (eligible for funding) follows as a valid modus ponens. No flaw.

difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a part-to-whole compositional fallacy. The answer choices span biology, economics, and linguistics, making topic-matching unhelpful. Two trap choices (A and C) involve whole-to-part division fallacies, which are the converse error, and one (B) presents a valid statistical inference, requiring careful structural diagnosis.
stimulus: Each individual coral polyp in the Great Barrier Reef is an extremely fragile organism, capable of being killed by a temperature increase of just one degree Celsius. Therefore, the Great Barrier Reef ecosystem as a whole must be extremely fragile, capable of being destroyed by a temperature increase of just one degree Celsius.
questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The national economy is highly resilient to short-term shocks, having recovered from every recession in the past century. Therefore, each individual business within the economy is highly resilient to short-term shocks.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In every clinical trial conducted over the past decade, the majority of patients who took Compound Z showed measurable improvement. Therefore, a patient chosen at random from a new trial is more likely than not to show improvement if given Compound Z.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The committee that drafted the new trade agreement is widely regarded as highly competent. Therefore, each individual member of that committee is probably highly competent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every neuron in a human brain processes signals at only a modest speed. Therefore, the brain as a whole processes information at only a modest speed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Each sentence in the novel is grammatically flawless. Therefore, the novel as a whole must be a literary masterpiece.

explanations.correct: The stimulus attributes a property of every individual part (fragility, one-degree vulnerability) to the whole system (the reef). Choice D does the same: every individual neuron (part) processes signals at only modest speed, therefore the whole brain processes information at only modest speed. This is the compositional fallacy — what is true of each part is assumed to be true of the whole — replicated precisely.
explanations.A: This is the division fallacy, the converse of the stimulus's error: attributing a property of the whole (national economy's resilience) to each part (individual businesses). The stimulus moves part → whole; this moves whole → part.
explanations.B: This is a valid probabilistic inference from aggregate trial data to an individual outcome probability. No fallacy is committed.
explanations.C: Like A, this is the division fallacy: attributing a property of the whole (the committee's reputation) to its individual members. The direction of inference is whole → part, opposite of the stimulus.
explanations.D: Correct. Matches the compositional fallacy: part (neuron) has property X → whole (brain) has property X.
explanations.E: Although this moves from parts to whole, the property shifts — grammatical flawlessness is not the same property as literary masterpiece. The stimulus attributes the same property (fragility / one-degree threshold) to both part and whole. Choice E involves an equivocation or scope shift, a different type of error.

difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a base-rate reversal: most members of group X have property Y, a thing has property Y, therefore the thing is probably a member of X. This is Carpaccio-tier difficulty. Answer choices share probabilistic vocabulary and cover economics, history, and biology. Trap choice B is valid; trap choice E reverses the flaw direction; trap choice A introduces a different flaw (correlation-causation).
stimulus: Most works that were celebrated by contemporary critics during the Harlem Renaissance were written by authors who had previously lived in the American South. The recently rediscovered novella Indigo Evenings was celebrated by contemporary critics during the Harlem Renaissance. Therefore, the author of Indigo Evenings had probably previously lived in the American South.
questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Companies that expand aggressively during economic downturns tend to gain significant market share. Hartwell Industries gained significant market share last quarter. Therefore, Hartwell Industries probably expanded aggressively during the most recent economic downturn.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most rivers that support thriving salmon populations have annual peak flows above two thousand cubic feet per second. The Calloway River has an annual peak flow above two thousand cubic feet per second. Therefore, the Calloway River probably supports a thriving salmon population.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most grant recipients in the university's science division have held a prior postdoctoral fellowship. Dr. Osei has held a prior postdoctoral fellowship. Therefore, Dr. Osei is probably a grant recipient in the university's science division.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A small number of investment funds that focus on emerging markets have consistently outperformed the broader index. The Meridian Fund focuses on emerging markets. Therefore, the Meridian Fund has probably consistently outperformed the broader index.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most poets who had previously lived in Paris during the 1920s produced work associated with the modernist movement. Jean Villeneuve produced work associated with the modernist movement and had previously lived in Paris. Therefore, Jean Villeneuve was probably celebrated by contemporary critics.

explanations.correct: Stimulus structure: Most [celebrated Harlem Renaissance works] → [author lived in South]; Indigo Evenings → [celebrated]; therefore [author lived in South]. The flaw: the conditional runs from celebrated works to Southern background, but the argument observes only that the work was celebrated and concludes the author had the Southern background. This is a base-rate reversal — P(Southern background | celebrated work) is used to infer P(celebrated work | Southern background). Choice C replicates this exactly: most grant recipients → prior fellowship; Dr. Osei → prior fellowship; therefore Dr. Osei → grant recipient. The property (prior fellowship) common to most members of a set is used to infer membership in the set from possession of the property.
explanations.A: Close trap, but the premise says companies that expand aggressively 'tend to' gain market share — this is a forward conditional (expand → gain share), and the argument affirms the consequent. The stimulus's premise also runs in a specific direction, but 'tend to' introduces a probabilistic hedge that shifts the structure. More importantly, the stimulus's flaw involves base-rate reversal from a 'most' claim about one set applied to infer membership in that set; A involves affirming the consequent of a tendency claim. Different flaw type.
explanations.B: This is a valid inference. The premise states most salmon-thriving rivers have high peak flow — but the conclusion is that the Calloway River supports salmon. This moves from having the property (high flow) to having a different property (salmon). The direction of the 'most' claim runs: salmon rivers → high flow; the argument observes high flow and concludes salmon. This IS a base-rate reversal — a strong trap. However, it differs from the stimulus in one key dimension: the stimulus's conclusion is about a property of the thing (author's background), while B's conclusion is about the thing's category membership. Wait — on re-examination, B is actually the same structural flaw and a strong competitor. But compared to C, B's premise says 'most rivers that support salmon have high flow,' and B concludes 'has high flow → supports salmon' — the reversal. C's premise says 'most grant recipients have fellowship,' and C concludes 'has fellowship → is grant recipient.' Both are the same flaw. The key differentiator: in the stimulus, the subject (the novella) was already confirmed to be in the reference class (celebrated Harlem Renaissance work), and the conclusion is about an additional property (author's background). In B, the subject is NOT confirmed in any class — the conclusion itself asserts class membership (supports salmon). In C, same as stimulus: the subject (Dr. Osei) is confirmed to have the property (fellowship), and the conclusion is about class membership (grant recipient). C mirrors the stimulus more precisely because the reference set (grant recipients) parallels the stimulus's reference set (celebrated works) and the shared property (fellowship / Southern background) is what bridges them.
explanations.C: Correct. Mirrors the stimulus's base-rate reversal: most members of set S have property P; individual X has property P; therefore X is probably in set S.
explanations.D: The premise uses 'a small number,' not 'most.' The flaw here is drawing a conclusion about a specific fund from a weak base rate (a small number outperform). This is a different error — reasoning from an existential or weak quantifier rather than from a 'most' claim. The stimulus's flaw depends critically on the 'most' quantifier.
explanations.E: This introduces a conclusion about critical celebration that was not in the premises about modernist movement or Paris residency. It chains two inferences (Paris → modernist; modernist → celebrated) without the second link being established. This is a non sequitur or unsupported additional inference, not a base-rate reversal. The stimulus only makes one inferential move.
